extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of humor theory, literary criticism, and psychology of comedy
extracted.subtask_description: A conceptual taxonomy and psychological account of humor: how sexuality, truth, quantity, irony, practical/poetic modes, and absurdity produce comic effect; includes examples (Aristophanes, Chaplin, Twain, Rabelais) and philosophical references (Freud, Kant, Aristotle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual underpinning of casual humor
rubrics_metrics.description: A great deal of our pleasure in the most casual humor is flavored with an emotion from the sphere of sex — our conscious attention being at play with the negative, while our unconscious takes its fill of a positive satisfaction we do not attend to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and examples: Persons of maidenly mind may laugh at a break in meaning that has a sexual implication of which they are not consciously aware; Freud claims many hilarious satisfactions are fundamentally sexual (the author credits Freud's illumination but cautions against overgeneralizing). Example anecdote: a child's paradoxical 'virtue brings its own reward' story illustrates unconscious satisfaction discharged in laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between glee and humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter arising from triumphant lust or battle cruelty (a loon-like hysterical giggle and whooping at cruel gibes and obscene quips) is glee, not humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Glee is a rank, ringing pleasure and is of no more special pertinence to the art of joking than any other kind of unsatisfied hunger; it is distinguished from companionable or artistic humor, which aims at revelation or playful insight rather than mere triumph or cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as revelation and release from self-consciousness (truthful shock)
rubrics_metrics.description: One chief source of the joy motive in popular jokes is Truth: to shock us with playful precipitation of the mist of pretense and, in that shock, warm us with a clear serious glimpse of the naked movement of life — allowing brief honest playfulness and relief from self-consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and examples: Humor offers a half-second of honesty comparable to ecstatic states; the author gives the speaker's absurd aside about the learned as an example of absurdity conjoined with interior truth. Aristophanes and Chaplin are cited as humorists who 'tell the plain truth of things' and make people conscious of reality by shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as a device to avoid or disarm serious truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor often serves as the last weapon of those menaced by truth: jokers meet serious thrusts with a flatly frivolous and irrelevant rebuff which conceals other serious satisfactions and permits attention to slide off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance/anti-pattern: Cicero advised using joking to dispose of ugly matters; conversely, one should not try to match wits with a professional joker — enjoy the joke and then return to serious speech so as not to be parried by evasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth is often the substance of humor (truth is humorous under civilized life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although 'humor is not truth,' truth, under the terms of civilized life, is humorous — humor frequently arises from bringing the plain sanity of a situation home to people by means of a shock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and illustration: Chaplin's comment that he tells the plain truth of things (e.g. slapping a contemptuous fine lady is 'really right') demonstrates humor's power to reveal a simpler reality and elicit laughter by exposing what people tacitly sense. This is a recommended interpretive stance for evaluating humor that 'uncovers' reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor of quantity — exaggeration and understatement as primary operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulating mere quantity or degree (making things too much or too little) produces humor: magnify a subject plausibly enough yet extremely enough to make belief impossible (exaggeration) or speak with words so slight as to be inadequate (understatement/irony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational guidance: These forms require agility of imagination rather than deep ingenuity. Examples: Rabelais and Mark Twain delight in mere quantity; Einstein's book-preface joke and Twain's 'reports of my death...' illustrate the comic effect of saying too little or too much to impracticability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony (taxonomy: understatement, overstatement, opposites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony properly names the elementary humor of understatement but has come to include jokes that say too little to mean much, say too much to mean little (overstatement), or state the exact opposite of what they mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and practical notes: Origin in Socratic 'saying little' that means much; Thorstein Veblen exemplifies sustained ironic ambiguity; the author recommends applying 'irony' primarily to understatement then to other quantitative jokes 'and there we ought to stop.' Examples: Socrates, Veblen, Charles Lamb's title 'On the Inconveniences Resulting from Being Hanged.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughing at impracticability — 'too much' or 'too little' is the comic trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh not at mere magnitude or minuteness, but at the point where quantity becomes impracticable — where 'too much' or 'too little' produces a real balk or bewilderment of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mark Twain's inflated pedometer punchline; the pedestrian who exclaims 'O Lord, this is too much!' when confronted with gross exaggeration. Use this as an evaluative criterion: the successful quantity-based joke leads the audience to experience that baffled 'too much' reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical humor (humor of disappointment and disturbance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical humor arises when a purposeful tendency toward an end is tripped up or brought to nothing (Kant's 'strained expectation brought to nothing') or when a present object is playfully disagreeable (Aristotle's 'harmlessly ugly').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinction and usage: Practical humor is the realm of jest, joke, wit, and the comic (practical, enterprise mood); it contrasts with poetic humor (ludicrous, droll). It need not be deliberately perpetrated (not simply 'practical jokes') — it requires only a practical discomfiture that can be taken playfully by observer or participant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity as the general name for practical negative humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurdity is the best general name for the practical kind of humor that is purely negative — a reduction-to-absurdity of the whole attitude of our wills where positive values are too fine to be identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and application: Situations like a horse refusing to move the family's Sunday vehicle become enormously comic; absurdity captures the negative, coming-to-nothing quality of such humor and is useful for evaluating 'practical' comedic scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Bull' or 'Irish bull' — plausible speech that lands on nothing
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'bull' is a remark that appears rotund and meaningful until apprehension arrives, when there is simply nothing there; its plausibility is the source of charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and implication: Such logical bubbles (Lewis Carroll, mathematical play) can be exquisitely humorous because the audience enjoys the dexterous landing of nothingness; useful when evaluating verbal absurdities and lightweight logical nonsense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony can function for praise as well as ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony is not necessarily hostile; by saying too much or too little the speaker can either deride or praise — conventionalized ironies convey opposite meanings through emphatic repetition or understatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and guidance: Phrases like 'He is some dancer!' can mean great praise by conventional emphasis, or 'He is a great dancer, he is!' can mean no dancer at all. When assessing irony, consider whether the ironic form is being used to commend as well as to satirize.
